This protracted juvenile phase is ecologically sensible given the species' reliance on diving for benthic prey, a foraging mode that requires substantial somatic growth and neuromuscular coordination before independent feeding is fully efficient. The relatively short incubation period is adaptive for Arctic-nesting birds, allowing chicks to hatch and begin growth during the brief summer window of high prey availability.

The larger body size of males may confer advantages in male-male competition for access to females during the breeding season, while the smaller female body mass may represent an energetic compromise that reduces the costs of egg production and incubation. When considered together, these mass values place the surf scoter among the medium-sized members of the tribe Mergini, with body sizes intermediate between the smaller bufflehead and the larger common eider.
